strengths: Soundness: The core continuous-time argument is convincing. Theorem 4.1 combines reverse-ODE stability, log-Sobolev regularization under the OU flow, and inexact Langevin convergence into an explicit Wasserstein error bound. The original target need not satisfy log-concavity or a log-Sobolev inequality.

Originality: Theorem 4.2 provides a useful technical contribution: clipping the terminal estimator around the Gaussian score converts L2 error control into the exponential-moment control required by the correction analysis.

Significance: Separating the forward diffusion horizon from the desired sampling accuracy gives useful theoretical understanding of initialization correction. The norm-subgaussian assumption covers a broad class of targets, including bounded distributions.

Presentation and limitations: The algorithm, error decomposition, and parameter roles are clearly explained, with detailed proofs in Appendices A–C. Section 6 explicitly acknowledges the incomplete discretization analysis. The theoretical and synthetic-data setting raises no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The advertised connection to standard training is stronger than established. Theorem 4.2 requires separate control of b(T1), which small time-integrated J_SM does not imply without additional uniform time regularity. Furthermore, the convergence discussion after Theorem 4.1 imposes stability across estimator sequences through integrals involving the one-sided Lipschitz constants. Although acknowledged, this condition does not follow from small L2 error. The concluding claim of convergence from control of the standard integrated loss should explicitly retain these requirements.

The full computational improvement remains unproved. Proposition 6.1 establishes the O(epsilon^-2 log(1/epsilon)) step count only for the Langevin initialization stage. A fixed reverse-ODE horizon does not control its discretization cost as the stopping time approaches zero or estimator Lipschitz constants grow. Likewise, the logarithmic dimension dependence concerns the required forward horizon; the complete bounds also contain dimension-dependent terms and potentially large stability factors.

Empirical reproducibility is inadequate. Figure 1 omits the chosen forward horizons, score-model architectures and training procedures, solver settings, sample counts, Wasserstein estimation procedure, and interpretation of the error bars. The three toy examples illustrate improvement with correction time, but provide no comparison at matched total computational cost and do not measure the exponential-moment error claimed to be small.

Several mathematical statements require correction. In Eqs. (3.3) and (3.5), the deterministic reverse case uses g multiplying the score, whereas consistency with (3.1) requires g^2/2. Also, Lemma 5.6's final KL bound is false as stated: for d=1, a point mass at sqrt(2/3), and t=(log 2)/2, its time condition holds but D_KL(gamma || p_t) is approximately 0.4868, exceeding 1/3. These appear locally repairable; the main OU theorem uses a stronger time condition.
